title: Rehabilitation after stroke: constraint-induced therapy
description: Constraint-induced movement therapy is an intensive rehabilitation method for an arm weakened by stroke: hours of daily practice with the weaker arm while the stronger one is restrained, plus a "transfer package" of techniques to carry the use of the weaker arm into daily life. In a randomised trial of people months or years after a stroke, those who had the full therapy used their weaker arm much more in daily life, and grey matter increased in the hand and arm areas for movement and sensation on both sides of the brain, and in the hippocampus. In this episode brightness stands for grey matter, not activity, and shows the change since before therapy.
caveat: The findings come from one randomised trial: 16 people received the full therapy and 20 the same therapy without the transfer package; the comparison group also improved, but showed no grey matter increases. The difference between groups was clear on one side and in the hippocampus, and only marginal on the other side. Eleven people with large strokes in the movement areas were left out of the movement-area analysis. The increases covered the hand and arm regions, the front of the supplementary motor area and part of the premotor area; the whole motor and sensory strips are drawn, which is larger than the areas that changed. Whether the changes last was not known. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.caption: Three hours a day of practice with the weaker arm on ten weekdays, the stronger arm restrained, and the transfer package. People were not scanned during this time.

phases.name: What changed

regions.explanation: Grey matter increased in the hand and arm area of the motor cortex on both sides after the full therapy, in a randomised trial.
